cards.name: Audience call-out ('If you're a...')
cards.summary: Open by naming the exact viewer: role plus situation ('If you're a CA still filing GST by hand...') or a place or community ('Indore walon...'), so the right person thinks 'that's me' in the first second and everyone else scrolls on. A good call-out is narrow enough to exclude people, and the rest of the piece serves only that person.
use_for: first 1-2 seconds (spoken line + on-screen text) of a reel or Short for a niche service
first line of a LinkedIn or Instagram caption before the 'more' cut
subject lines for a segmented email list ('For Shopify sellers under Rs 1 crore')
local business promos aimed at one city or neighbourhood
the eyebrow line above a landing-page headline
avoid: Broad call-outs that exclude nobody ('If you're an entrepreneur...', 'Hey everyone'): narrow to role + situation + stake, e.g. 'D2C founders whose RTO is above 20%'.

Paid Meta ads that call out a condition or status ('Diabetic ho?', 'In debt?'): Meta bans ads that assert or imply personal attributes. Lead with the product or situation instead ('Sugar-free mithai for Diwali').
Calling out two audiences in one hook ('students and working professionals'): pick one, make a second version for the other.
A call-out the body ignores: if the hook says 'Pune landlords', every example in the body must be a Pune landlord's.
templates: If you're a [role] who [specific situation], [promise or warning].
If you [did X in the last N days], watch this before [deadline/decision].
examples: If you're a CA in a tier-2 city still filing GST returns by hand, this setup gives you your Sundays back.
Jaipur walon, is Sunday MI Road mat jaana. Detour ye raha.
Shopify sellers with COD above 60%: your return problem starts at checkout, not at delivery.
First-time home buyers in Pune: read this before you pay the token amount.
Agar aap freelancer ho aur client 60 din se payment nahi kar raha, ye email bhejo.
cards.why_it_works: Naming the viewer filters the audience: the people the piece is not for leave early, and the people it is for feel it was made for them and stay for the payoff. It is a long-standing headline move: Copyblogger lists 'If you're [X], you can [Y]' among its 22 formulas and Caples' benefit headlines include ones addressed to a specific audience (Lofgren's summary). CreatorsJet pairs the call-out with a specific mistake ('If you are [viewer], stop doing [mistake]') so the identity line also carries tension.
cards.risk: Broken promise when the hook promises advice for one specific group and the body is generic advice for everyone. Clickbait when the call-out is fake-narrow ('Only people born in March will get this'). Legal line: in Meta (Facebook/Instagram) ads the call-out must not assert or imply a personal attribute such as health, financial status, religion or age; Meta's own disallowed example is 'Are you bankrupt? Check out our services.' (comp:meta_advertising_standards). Organic posts are not bound by that ad rule, but a boosted post is an ad.

cards.name: Before-and-after / transformation
cards.summary: Show or state the after first (the cleaned-up kitchen, the 4.8-star listing, the paid-off card), cut to the before, and promise the bridge. Good versions make both states concrete and checkable, use the real result of the real product, and deliver the method in the body.
use_for: reel and Short openers for home makeovers, design, editing, cleaning, organising and small-business fixes
UGC and Meta ad hooks where the change is visible on camera
landing-page hero for a service with a visible outcome
avoid: Health, weight-loss, skin and hair transformations in ads: Meta bans statements of inferiority about appearance and timed results without qualifiers, and drug or remedy claims fall under the DMR Act. Show the process or a documented customer result with its conditions instead.
An 'after' produced by lighting, filters, a different person or a best-ever case presented as typical: show a typical result or state the conditions in the same language and font.
A big reveal with no bridge: if the body never explains what changed, use a plain before/after carousel without a hook claim.
Invented numbers in the hook: use the client's real before/after figures and their time window, or no numbers.
templates: [After state]. [Time] ago it looked like this. Here's what changed.
From [before metric] to [after metric] (in [period], only when the change took time): [method in 3-5 words].
Pehle: [before]. Ab: [after]. Farak sirf [one change] ka hai.
examples: Ye 1BHK ka kitchen hai. Teen weekend pehle aisa dikhta tha. Total kharcha Rs 18,400.
Our Meesho listing went from 2 orders a week to 2 a day. The only change was the first photo.
Before: 14 browser tabs and a notebook to plan a shaadi budget. After: one sheet. Template in the comments.
Pehle: har mahine Rs 3,000 late fee. Ab: zero. Farak sirf ek auto-debit date ka hai.
cards.why_it_works: The contrast makes the change visible in one glance, and leading with the after shows the payoff first, so the viewer stays to learn the bridge. TrueFan describes the reel version as flashing the after briefly and then jumping to the before; CreatorsJet uses 'Before and after: [old way] vs [new way]' as quick visual proof. The full-piece structure is fw:bab.
cards.risk: Tips into a broken promise when the after is staged, edited or not typical, or when the body never shows how to get there. Legal line in India: an ad's result claim must be capable of substantiation and any 'results vary' disclaimer must be in the same language and font and may clarify but not contradict the claim (CCPA 2022, comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022). Health and appearance: Meta bans inferiority statements and timed outcomes without qualifiers (comp:meta_advertising_standards); drug or remedy cures are criminal under the DMR Act 1954 (comp:dmr_act_1954); coaching results need rank, course and paid-status disclosure plus written consent (comp:ccpa_coaching_ads_2024).

cards.name: Bold claim / big promise
cards.summary: State the outcome outright: 'Now you can [result] without [the usual cost]'. A good bold promise is one specific result the reader wants, believable for where they are, and provable in the body or the offer; the reader knows in one line what they get.
use_for: Google Ads RSA and Meta ad headlines
launch and promotional email subject lines
YouTube titles for a tutorial with a clear outcome
app store and product listing first lines
avoid: Superlatives and guarantees the client cannot prove on paper ('India's best', 'guaranteed results'): replace with the specific, provable result ('ITR filed in 15 minutes, checked by a CA').
Promising a result to readers who do not yet know they have the problem: open with the problem (hook:problem_solution or fw:pas) and save the promise for line two.
Stacking three promises in one line: keep the one the buyer cares about most, move the rest to subheads.
Coaching, finance and health promises: 'guaranteed selection', 'double your money', 'lose 10 kg in 10 days' are restricted or banned; promise the process, not the outcome.
templates: Now you can [specific result] without [usual pain or cost].
Get [specific result] - [proof element: number, guarantee, name].
examples: Now you can file your ITR from WhatsApp, without a single visit to the CA's office.
Your restaurant menu as a QR code, live in one afternoon. No app, no developer.
Ab bolo Hindi mein, invoice khud ban jayega.
Clean, RO-grade drinking water for a family of four at Rs 3 a day.
cards.why_it_works: Ogilvy (quoted by Copyblogger): five times as many people read the headline as the body, so the headline has to carry the benefit on its own. Lofgren's summary of Caples says benefit-focused headlines give the most sales for the least effort. Ogilvy also warns against tricky or irrelevant headlines: the plain promise is the opposite of a trick.
cards.risk: The line between bold and false is substantiation. In India every objectively factual claim must be capable of substantiation (CCPA 2022 cl. 12, comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022; ASCI Code Ch I.1, comp:asci_code); obvious hyperbole is allowed only when nobody would read it literally. Coaching ads may not promise selection, rank or jobs (comp:ccpa_coaching_ads_2024). Google Ads rejects 'an improbable result (even if this result is possible) as the likely outcome' (comp:google_ads_misrepresentation), and Meta rejects promises of specific outcomes within a set timeframe without qualifiers.

cards.name: Quiz / spot-the-mistake opener
cards.summary: Turn the opener into a test the viewer plays: 'Can you spot the mistake in 3 seconds?'. A good one shows a frame where the mistake is genuinely findable, gives the answer on time, and teaches why it is a mistake.
use_for: reels and Shorts on design, fashion, grammar, form, invoices, scams and safety
carousel slide 1 with the answer on slide 2 or 3
LinkedIn document posts and quiz posts
training content (spot the error in this form or bill)
avoid: Surfaces with nothing to inspect (email subject, audio-only): use hook:question instead.
Withholding the answer to farm comments ('answer in comments'): give it in the piece; ask for their guess before the reveal.
Puzzles that are trivial or impossible: test with two people from the audience first; one should get it, one should not.
Ego-bait claims ('only geniuses can spot this', '1% will get it'): the number is invented; drop it.
templates: Can you spot the mistake in [N] seconds?
Is [thing] mein [N] galtiyan hain. Kitni dikhi?
One of these [items] is [fake/wrong]. Which one?
Find the [error type] before I do.
examples: Is GST invoice mein ek galti hai jo notice dilwa sakti hai. 3 second. Dikhi?
Can you spot what's wrong with this resume in 5 seconds?
Two of these three 'Banarasi' sarees are powerloom. Which one is handloom?
Spot the scam: one of these SMS is from your bank, one is from a fraudster.
cards.why_it_works: A task gives the viewer a reason to keep looking and a small reward for being right, and the reveal is a built-in payoff at a known moment. TrueFan lists it as the '3-Second Challenge' India reel format ('Can you spot the mistake in 3 seconds?') running in the first 3 seconds.
cards.risk: Clickbait when the mistake is not actually in the frame, when the answer is never given, or when a fake difficulty statistic is attached. If the 'mistake' is in a named competitor's product or ad, it becomes comparative advertising: honest, verifiable and non-denigrating only (comp:trade_marks_comparative_ads, comp:asci_code).

cards.name: Case-study title
cards.summary: Lead with the measured result, then the method, then the label: '[Result with number]: how we [method] (case study)'. Good: the number is real and client-approved, has a baseline and a time window, and the body shows the steps that produced it.
use_for: YouTube titles for agency or creator breakdowns
avoid: Percentages without a base ('300% growth' from 3 to 12 leads): give both numbers ('from 40 to 310 leads a month').
Vanity metrics (impressions, followers) when the buyer pays for revenue, leads or cost saved: lead with the money metric.
Results the client has not approved for publication: get written sign-off on numbers and name, or anonymise ('a Jaipur CA firm').
The best client presented as typical: say it is one client, or give the range.
examples: From 40 to 310 leads a month: how a Jaipur CA firm rebuilt its Google Business Profile (case study)
How a Pune ghee brand cut RTO from 28% to 11% with one WhatsApp confirmation step
Rs 0 ad spend, 1,200 pre-orders: a Kolhapuri chappal launch, step by step
Kota coaching centre ki enquiries 3 mahine mein double: kya badla (case study)
cards.why_it_works: Proof first answers 'does this work?' before the reader asks it, and the method promise gives the reason to click. Backlinko's 'Skyscraper Method: +110% Traffic (Link Building Case Study)' is a well-known instance of the pattern: result number, method, label.
cards.risk: Broken promise when the body hides the method behind a call booking or when the result came from something other than the named method. Legal line in India: a result claim used to sell must be capable of substantiation (CCPA 2022, comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022) and a client quote is an endorsement that must reflect genuine experience. Coaching and ed-tech results must disclose the student's rank, course and whether it was paid, with written consent for name or photo (comp:ccpa_coaching_ads_2024). US clients: comp:ftc_consumer_reviews_rule.

cards.name: Challenge / experiment ('I tried X for 30 days')
cards.summary: A first-person experiment with a fixed rule and timeframe: 'I tried [X] for [N] days', 'I tested the cheap one'. Good: the rule is clear, the test was actually run as stated, the days are documented, and the result is reported honestly, including a flop.
use_for: reel series that post day-by-day updates
LinkedIn and newsletter posts by founders and creators
UGC ad hooks ('I tested the Rs 400 one for a month')
avoid: Tests compressed or faked (30 days filmed in one weekend): the audience notices and the comments say so; shorten the claim ('one weekend') instead.
Challenges with a health risk (crash diets, extreme fasting, sleep deprivation): pick a safe rule, and keep timed body results out of ads.
Saving every result for the last second: give a midpoint result so the viewer has a reason to stay.
A paid creator's 'test' presented as independent: disclose the paid partnership up front.
templates: I tried [X] for [N] days. Here's what happened.
I [did X] every day for [N] days so you don't have to.
I tested [cheap option] vs [expensive option] for [N] weeks.
[N] din tak sirf [X]. Result dekh lo.
examples: I paid for everything by UPI only for 30 days. Here's where Rs 6,200 leaked.
30 din tak roz 5 baje utha. Productivity nahi badhi, kuch aur badla.
I ordered the same thali from five cloud kitchens in Lucknow. Only one was cooked fresh.
I tested the Rs 400 and the Rs 4,000 trimmer for a month. Here's the honest answer.
cards.why_it_works: A fixed rule plus a time window builds a story arc into the title (setup, struggle, result) and a question the viewer wants answered: did it work? Matt Cutts' TED talk on trying something new for 30 days is the widely known template of the frame; Zeely lists 'I tested'-style openers among native TikTok ad hooks.
cards.risk: Broken promise when the test was not run as stated or the result is spun. In ads, a creator's 'I tried it' is an endorsement: it must reflect genuine, reasonably current use and any material connection must be disclosed (CCPA 2022 cl. 13-14, comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022; comp:asci_influencer; US: comp:ftc_endorsement_guides). Body-result challenges in Meta ads hit the timed-outcome rule (comp:meta_advertising_standards).

cards.name: Command headline
cards.summary: Open with a verb that tells the reader what to do: 'Stop...', 'Try...', 'Read this before you...'. A good command names the action and the situation ('Before you renew car insurance, check the IDV line'), so the reader knows why it applies to them; a generic command ('Stop scrolling') does not.
use_for: email subject lines and push notifications
Google Ads headlines that double as the CTA
avoid: Generic commands ('Stop scrolling', 'Watch till the end'): add the specific reason or switch to hook:audience_callout.
Bossy commands to cold senior B2B readers: a question or a plain descriptive line reads as more respectful.
ALL-CAPS commands in search ads ('BUY NOW'): Google Ads Editorial rejects gimmicky capitalisation.
Guilt or fear lines on decline buttons ('No thanks, I like losing money'): that is confirm shaming.
templates: Save this before your next [event]. (Instagram / carousel only)
[Kaam] karne se pehle ye dekh lo.
examples: Before you renew your car insurance this month, check the IDV line.
Stop writing 'Dear Sir/Madam' in cold emails. Use their first name.
Flat book karne se pehle society ka maintenance ledger maang lo.
Save this before your next Meesho product shoot.
cards.why_it_works: A verb hands the reader a role in the first word, and a specific action implies there is a concrete reason the body will give. Copyblogger's command templates ('See how easily you can...', '[Do something] like [world-class example]') are classic forms; Insense notes that a specific command ('Before you buy another X, watch this') beats a generic one ('Stop scrolling').
cards.risk: Broken promise when the body never justifies the command. On decline links and pop-ups, a shaming command is a banned dark pattern in India (confirm shaming, CCPA 2023, comp:ccpa_dark_patterns_2023). In Google search ads keep commands in normal case and punctuation (comp:google_ads_editorial).

cards.name: Comparison (X vs Y)
cards.summary: Pit two options the reader is actually choosing between against each other: '[A] vs [B]: which wins for [use]?'. Good: the criteria are named, the test is fair, and the piece ends with a verdict or a clear 'it depends on X'.
use_for: comparison articles that target 'X vs Y' searches
reels on cheap vs expensive, old way vs new way
sales pages comparing the old process with the product
carousels with one criterion per slide
avoid: A straw-man rival nobody would pick: compare against the option the buyer is really weighing.
No verdict: if it truly depends, name the deciding factor ('under Rs 12 lakh salary, the new regime wins').
Ads that name a rival brand to mock it: compare verifiable facts (price, spec, tested result) in plain text, never its logo, colours or tagline.
Rigged tests (best of yours vs worst of theirs): use the same conditions and say what they were.
templates: Rs [cheap] vs Rs [expensive] [product]: worth the extra?
[A] or [B]? I used both for [N] weeks.
examples: Term plan vs ULIP at 30: the three numbers that decide it
Rs 400 vs Rs 4,000 mixer grinder: kaunsa 5 saal chalega?
Electric vs petrol scooter in Bengaluru traffic: monthly cost, compared
Old tax regime vs new: kis salary pe kaunsa?
cards.why_it_works: It mirrors a decision the reader is already making and promises to shortcut their research; two named options make the topic clear in one glance. CreatorsJet frames it as 'Here is the difference between [A] and [B]' for two ideas people confuse; Zeely lists comparison openers among TikTok ad hooks.
cards.risk: Broken promise when there is no verdict or the criteria are hidden. Legal line in India: naming a competitor's registered trade mark in advertising is lawful only in accordance with honest practices and without taking unfair advantage of or harming its reputation (Trade Marks Act s.29(8), s.30(1)); a voice-over naming the rival counts too (s.29(9)) (comp:trade_marks_comparative_ads). Comparisons must be substantiated (CCPA 2022 cl. 12) and must not denigrate (ASCI Code Ch IV.1.5).

cards.summary: State an opinion against the niche's standard advice ('Your startup does not need a pitch deck yet') and then defend it with reasons, evidence and the replacement advice. Good: the writer genuinely holds the view, it survives the strongest counter-argument, and the reader leaves with something to do instead.
use_for: reels that correct generic advice in a niche
avoid: Rage-bait the client does not believe: if they would not defend it in a meeting, do not post it.
Contradicting advice that is right on safety, health, tax or investing: the cost of being wrong lands on the reader.
Critique with no replacement: CreatorsJet's version is 'What [creator] should do instead of [tactic]'.
A take that ends by agreeing with the norm ('...unless you do it right'): that is a broken promise; pick a real disagreement or use hook:myth_busting.
templates: Everyone says [X]. I [did the opposite] and [result].
[Common advice] doesn't work for [audience]. Do [replacement] instead.
Sab bolte hain [X]. Main bolta hoon [Y], aur reason ye hai.
examples: Unpopular opinion: your startup does not need a pitch deck for its first Rs 50 lakh. It needs 10 paying customers.
Stop asking clients for 'feedback'. Ask them one question instead.
Sab bolte hain roz post karo. Humne hafte mein 2 kiye aur enquiries badhi.
Everyone says Hindi content doesn't sell B2B. Our best lead this year came from a Hindi reel.
cards.why_it_works: Disagreement with a familiar belief creates tension: the reader checks their own view and stays to see the argument. CreatorsJet's opinion-led formula ('Most creators get [topic] wrong because [reason]') adds the condition that makes it work: the reason must be defensible. Sourcing is thin (practitioner reel guides only).
cards.risk: Tips into clickbait when the take is manufactured for engagement and the body quietly agrees with the norm. Finance takes from unregistered creators touch SEBI's finfluencer restrictions (comp:sebi_finfluencer_association); takes on religion, caste or communities can cross India's promoting-enmity and defamation provisions (comp:bns_defamation_speech). Name ideas, not private people.

cards.name: Curiosity gap
cards.summary: Reveal enough to show the reader there is something specific they don't know, and promise to close that gap if they read or watch on. Good gaps are concrete (a named object, place, number or line) and are closed early and fully in the piece.
use_for: YouTube titles and the thumbnail text that pairs with them
newsletter and promotional email subject lines
X and LinkedIn post first lines
article headlines for features (not for how-to search pages)
avoid: Teasers with no concrete noun ('You won't believe what happened'): name the thing ('the one line in your rent agreement...').
Gaps the piece never closes or closes with something trivial: the payoff must be worth the click.

Paid search and social ads: Google and Meta reject clickbait and sensational teasers; state the benefit instead.
templates: The [specific thing] [audience] check before [action] (most skip it)
What [specific group] know about [topic] that [other group] don't
examples: The one line in your rent agreement that decides if you get your deposit back

Bank ne ye SMS bheja tha. Maine ignore kiya. Galti thi.
Why your Rs 299 order costs Rs 337 at checkout
cards.why_it_works: George Loewenstein's information-gap account of curiosity (Psychological Bulletin, 1994) holds that curiosity arises when attention is drawn to a gap in what we know, and people act to close it. A specific subject makes the gap feel closable; a 2024 Scientific Reports paper studies when curiosity-gap headlines backfire depending on concreteness (only its title was read, so no finding is claimed here).
cards.risk: This family is the definition of clickbait when it goes wrong: Wikipedia describes a teaser as exploiting the curiosity gap and clickbait as typically deceptive or sensationalised. The line is crossed when the payoff is missing, trivial or different from what was implied. cards.name: Plain descriptive subject line
cards.summary: Say exactly what is inside, in plain words, with no tricks: 'Your October statement and a change to late-fee dates'. Good: the reader can decide whether to open without opening, the key noun comes first, and the email delivers exactly that.
use_for: newsletters to an engaged list (topic, not issue number)
WhatsApp template and push-notification first lines
avoid: Vague labels ('Update', 'Newsletter #47', 'Important information'): name the topic and the one thing the reader must know or do.
Cold or promotional sends where plain description gives no reason to open: add the benefit or the number ('Diwali cut-off dates + free gift wrap till 20 Oct').
Fake 'Re:' or 'Fwd:' to look descriptive of a conversation that never happened: it is a misleading header.
Long subjects that hide the key word past the cut-off: Mailchimp recommends no more than 9 words and 60 characters.
examples: Your October statement and a change to late-fee dates

cards.risk: Little clickbait risk; the failure is vagueness or dullness on a cold list. Legal line: US CAN-SPAM requires that 'the subject line must accurately reflect the content of the message' and bans misleading header information (comp:can_spam). cards.name: Emoji / symbol subject line
cards.summary: One emoji that adds meaning beside the words (a parcel for 'shipped', a diya for Diwali), never replacing a word. Good: the subject reads complete with the emoji removed, and it has been tested in the main inboxes the list uses.
use_for: push notifications and WhatsApp template first lines
avoid: Formal B2B, legal, financial-notice, medical and condolence emails: no emoji.
An emoji standing in for a word ('Your order has [parcel]'): it may render as an empty box; write the word.
More than one emoji: Mailchimp's guidance is no more than 1 at a time.
Urgency emoji (siren, alarm clock) on an offer with no real deadline: that is false urgency.
Copying an emoji subject into a Google search ad: symbols used for decoration are rejected there.
An emoji that adds a claim the words do not make (a check mark on 'status updated' reads as 'approved'; a gift box with no gift): the emoji must match the news.

cards.name: Fear of missing out (FOMO)
cards.summary: Signal that others are already in, or that the moment is passing, and the reader is about to miss it. Good FOMO is true and specific: the real number of people, the real date, the real seats or stock left.
use_for: festival campaigns tied to a real date (Diwali, Raksha Bandhan, ITR due date)
avoid: Fake counters ('27 people are viewing this'), fake stock and deadlines that reset: these are banned in India; use the real figure or none.
Evergreen products with no real moment: use hook:bold_promise or hook:social_proof.
Teen, health-anxiety and debt audiences: fear of missing out lands as pressure; use calm, factual copy.
Vague crowds ('everyone is switching'): give the count and the group ('412 Indore bakers').
templates: [Real number] [peer group] have already [done X]. [Real deadline or what's left].
[Real number] [group] asked us about [X] this week. Here's the 60-second version.
examples: 412 Indore bakers have already listed on the app. Registration closes 15 Nov.

cards.why_it_works: Fear of missing out is apprehension that others are having rewarding experiences or information one lacks (Wikipedia); a peer group plus a closing date turns that into a reason to act now. TrueFan lists 'Festival FOMO' ('Diwali ke pehle yeh setting change kar lo') among India reel hooks.
cards.risk: The legal line in India is explicit: CCPA's Dark Patterns Guidelines 2023 ban false urgency, i.e. falsely stating or implying scarcity or popularity; the gazette's own illustration is 'Only 2 rooms left! 30 others are looking at this right now' when untrue (comp:ccpa_dark_patterns_2023). cards.name: Hinglish mistake hook ('Ye galti mat karna')
cards.summary: The Hinglish 'don't make this mistake' opener: 'Ye galti mat karna', 'Mat karo yeh...', 'Zyaadatar log yahan galti karte hain'. It names one costly, common mistake in the viewer's own spoken mix of Hindi and English, like a friend's warning, and the fix arrives in the next line or two.
use_for: reels and Shorts for Hindi-belt and tier-2/3 audiences
personal finance, government scheme, property, shaadi and small-business tips

avoid: Invented percentages ('99% log ye galti karte hain'): unless the client has a sourced figure, say 'zyaadatar log' or name the situation.
Metro English-first B2B audiences: use hook:mistake_warning in English.

Running it on every post of a page: rotate with question, before-after and myth formats so it does not become wallpaper.
Mixing scripts at random: match the page's script (Roman Hinglish or Devanagari) and keep it the same in VO captions and on-screen text.

Zyaadatar log [task] mein yahi galti karte hain.
[Cheez] lene se pehle ye ek galti avoid karo.
examples: Car loan sign karne se pehle ye galti mat karna: insurance wala line item padh lo.
Shaadi ka venue book karte waqt ye galti mat karna. Cancellation clause pehle padho.
Mat karo yeh: resume mein 'hardworking' likhna. Uski jagah ek number likho.
Online dukaan kholi hai? Zyaadatar log pehli photo mein yahi galti karte hain.
cards.why_it_works: The mistake frame triggers a self-check ('am I doing this?'), and code-switching between colloquial Hindi and English (Wikipedia's definition of Hinglish) makes it sound like advice from a friend rather than an ad. cards.risk: Tips into clickbait when the 'galti' is not a real or common mistake, when the fix is withheld, or when a made-up statistic is attached. cards.name: Mid-action / mid-sentence opener

use_for: reel and Short openers for story and explainer content

A staged 'real' moment in an ad that pretends to be user content: label it as an ad.

cards.risk: Broken promise when the dramatic middle is invented or the story never returns to explain it. An ad dressed as a candid user moment or news clip is a disguised advertisement, a banned dark pattern in India (comp:ccpa_dark_patterns_2023); disclose that it is an ad.

cards.name: Aspirational comparison ('like a pro')

cards.name: Long descriptive headline
cards.summary: A full-sentence headline that states topic, benefit and angle in one go, 14-20 words (Backlinko's share band is 14-17). Good: every word adds information (who, what, result, where), it reads as one natural sentence, and it sits on a surface that shows the whole line.
use_for: LinkedIn articles and newsletter web titles
link posts on Facebook and LinkedIn
avoid: Surfaces that cut the line: YouTube titles cap at 100 characters, and Mailchimp recommends subject lines of no more than 9 words and 60 characters. Use hook:keyword_front_loaded or hook:short_punchy there.
Padding with adjectives to reach length ('The ultimate, complete, definitive...'): length should come from facts, not hype.
Two sentences pretending to be one headline: move the second to the dek.
Past 20 words: drop the ', and what [audience] can copy' / 'what it means for' tail; it is optional.
Customer-facing launch posts: drop the what-[other audience]-can-copy tail; it speaks to competitors, not buyers.

What [time] of [doing X] in [place] taught us about [A], [B] and [C]
Why [surprising finding], and what it means for [audience] in [year]
[Product] for [audience] who [situation]: [what is in it], [where / when]

cards.name: Myth-busting
cards.summary: Name a belief the audience really holds and show it is false: 'Myth: [X]. Fact: [Y]'. Good: the myth is common in this audience, the fact is correct and sourced on screen or in the caption, and the piece ends with what to do now.
use_for: explainers on money, tax, government schemes, tech, food and home

LinkedIn posts that correct industry folklore
avoid: Straw myths nobody believes: pick ones from real comments, search queries or customer calls.
'Facts' without a source: name the source (the Act, the official portal, the regulator) in the caption or on screen.
Leaving the myth as the biggest text: make the fact the headline-sized line, so a skimmer leaves with the fact.
Health myth-busting that ends in a product cure claim: that is an ad under the DMR Act and Meta health rules, not a myth-buster.
templates: You've been told [X]. Here's what [source] actually says.

In ads, implying that professionals or institutions hide something is an unsubstantiated claim (CCPA 2022, comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022); paired with a health product it can become a prohibited cure claim (comp:dmr_act_1954).
